description:
In this talk, Joseph Okaly challenges one of the most common assumptions about personal finance: that budgeting is the key to building wealth. Drawing from personal experience and years working with families, he explains why traditional budgeting often leads to frustration without meaningful progress.

Instead, he introduces a simple but powerful shift in thinking: flipping the “budgeting equation” from income - spending = saving to income - saving = spending.

By prioritizing saving first and automating the process, individuals can create a more sustainable, less stressful approach to money.

Through personal stories, including his mother’s financial journey, and real-world examples, this talk highlights how small behavioral changes, such as improving savings by even 1%, can compound into meaningful long-term wealth and greater peace of mind. author: TEDx Talks
description:
What I Learned About Change After Losing the Only Identity I Knew

What do you do next when your career is disrupted, your business fails, or your identity crumbles?

Former Seattle Seahawks safety Jordan Babineaux faced this exact crisis. After a decade in the NFL, including a Super Bowl appearance, his career ended without warning. COVID took his business and his mother. Then, soon later, he lost a brother.

Standing in the wreckage of his life, Jordan discovered what most people get wrong about navigating change: we wait for a crisis to force our hand instead of pivoting with intention.

In this talk, Jordan shares:

Why we're more afraid of success than failure (and how to fix it)
The critical question that separates stuck leaders from resilient ones
How to rebuild your identity without starting from scratch
If you've ever felt stuck between who you were and who you're becoming, this 10-minute talk will show you how to pivot with purpose before life forces your hand. Jordan Babine
title: What I learned about courage after losing my identity | Jordan Babineaux | TEDxEustis

description:
Why do we fear death so much? In this honest and unexpected talk, Luke, a grade eleven student, shares personal stories, from shaving his great-grandfather’s beard to meeting a preserved grandmother in a Fujian mountain home. Through these moments, he asks us to rethink how distant we’ve become from death—and what we might be missing because of it.
He points out that in many traditions, death was close. People talked to the dead, slept near them, and cared for their bodies. Now, those moments are handed over to professionals. With that shift came fear. Luke speaks openly and with humor, reminding us that dead bodies aren’t unsafe, and grief doesn’t have to be rushed. Sometimes, staying close to death is the best way to feel alive. NAIS G11 Student This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community.
